title: EST English — Full Practice Test 6
kicker: American Diploma · EST I · Practice test
summary: A full, timed EST I English practice test: Literacy Test 1 (Writing and Language, 44 questions, 35 minutes) and Literacy Test 2 (Reading, 52 questions, 65 minutes), with an explanation for every answer and every choice.

blocks.text: This is a complete practice version of the two English parts of EST I: **Literacy Test 1 (Writing and Language)** and **Literacy Test 2 (Reading)**. Every passage and question was written for this site by Mohamed Abdelkriem. The test is modelled on the skills that the EST Literacy tests measure; it is not made of official EST questions, and the real test may present questions in a different way.

rows: Four essays (Chinese silk, a solar park near Aswan, rice-duck farming, baking bread in a village) with numbered, underlined parts. Fix grammar and punctuation, and improve transitions, order, wording and relevance.

Five long passages (village fiction, ancient Greek history, science with a table, a pair of opinion texts about food, the history of paper). Answer questions about ideas, details, words, structure, evidence and data.

blocks.text: These figures are as published by schools; check the latest official EST candidate guide on est.moe.gov.eg before your test.

items: Sit in a quiet place with no phone, no dictionary and no help, exactly as in the real test.
Do the two sections in one sitting if you can. The timer starts when you begin each section and the section ends when the time is up.
Work through the questions in order. You can mark a question and come back to it while the section is still open, but once a section ends you cannot return to it, just as in the real test.
Answer every question. A blank is always wrong; a careful guess may be right.

Each passage is repeated above each of its questions. In Literacy Test 1, only the part that question asks about is underlined and numbered. In Literacy Test 2, the paragraphs are numbered [1], [2], [3] so that questions can point to them.
At the end you see a practice percentage for each section. It is not an official EST scaled score; use it to measure your progress from one practice test to the next.

questions.p:
**The Thread That Crossed the World**
More than four thousand years ago, farmers in China discovered that a small, pale caterpillar could give them one of the most valuable materials in history. The caterpillar, known as the silkworm, feeds only on the leaves of the mulberry tree. When it is ready to change into a moth, it wraps itself in a cocoon spun from a single unbroken thread__[1], that__ can be hundreds of metres long. To make silk, workers boiled the cocoons, find the end of the thread and unwind it carefully onto a reel. Several threads are then twisted together to make a yarn strong enough for weaving.
For many centuries, China kept the method a closely guarded secret. Silk cloth travelled west along the trade routes that later became known as the Silk Road, and wealthy buyers as far away as Rome paid high prices for it. However, those buyers had little idea how the fabric was made; some Roman writers believed that silk was combed from the leaves of trees. The rulers of China protected the secret carefully because of the reason that the trade brought them enormous wealth.
According to a well-known story, the secret finally escaped in the sixth century CE. The Byzantine emperor Justinian, whose capital was Constantinople wanted to stop paying Persian merchants for Chinese silk. Two monks who had travelled in the East offered to help. They returned with silkworm eggs hidden inside hollow walking sticks, and before long silk was being produced within the empire's own borders. 
Even after the secret spread, Chinese silk remained super popular with loads of people. The skills of Chinese weavers, who could create patterned fabrics of great complexity, was still admired across Asia and beyond. Today, scientists are even studying silk for use in medicine, because the material is strong, light. And gentle on human tissue. From mulberry leaves in ancient Chinese villages to modern laboratories, the silkworm's thread has travelled a very long way.
questions.q: [1] Choose the best version of the underlined part.
c: NO CHANGE
: that
that
; that
questions.e: "That can be hundreds of metres long" is an essential clause describing the thread, so it takes no punctuation. The strongest trap, the comma, wrongly cuts the noun off from the clause that identifies it; semicolons and colons need a complete sentence around them.
ce: A comma should not separate a noun from a "that" clause that identifies it.
A colon cannot introduce a "that" clause that simply describes the noun before it.
No punctuation is needed: "that can be hundreds of metres long" is essential information about the thread.
A semicolon must join two complete sentences; "that can be hundreds of metres long" is not one.

**Sunlight on the Sand**
Not far from the city of Aswan, in southern Egypt, millions of dark panels stretch across the desert in long, straight rows. This is the Benban Solar Park, one of the largest groups of solar power plants in the world. Covering more than thirty square kilometres, __[1] visitors are often amazed by the park's size__. Instead of a single giant power station, the park is made up of dozens of separate plants, each built and run by its own company.
Southern Egypt is an excellent place to collect energy from the sun. The region has three great advantages. Strong sunshine, flat land and very little rain. **Partners in the Paddy**
In many rice-growing regions of Asia, farmers rely on an unusual team of helpers: ducks. Farmers in southern China have kept ducks in their rice fields for centuries, and the practice is also found in Japan, Korea and other parts of Asia. The method may sound old-fashioned, __[1] but, it solves__ several problems at once.
The ducklings are released into the flooded fields a week or two after the young rice plants are set out in the fields where they will grow. As they paddle between the rows, they eat weeds and insects that would otherwise damage the crop. Their droppings, meanwhile, add natural fertiliser to the water. 
For the farmer, the ducks bring more than a cleaner field. When the rice is ready to harvest, the ducks are fully grown and can be sold, this means the same field produces two crops instead of one. Farmers who use the method also spend less money on chemical sprays, since they are rarely needed. In addition, their rice can often be sold at a higher price to customers who prefer food grown without such chemicals.
The method does have its difficulties. Ducks must be protected from foxes, dogs and birds of prey, so farmers often surround their fields with low fences and give the ducks a shelter for the night. Foxes are known for their bushy tails and pointed ears. When the rice begins to form grains, the ducks must be kicked out of the fields, because they would otherwise eat the rice itself.
Today, interest in rice-duck farming is growing again. Particularly among farmers who want to reduce their use of chemicals. Some researchers have reported that well-managed fields with ducks can produce harvests as large as conventional fields. In the end, the oldest methods are always the best ones.

questions.p:
**Bread in the Sun**
Every summer, my family left Cairo to spend a month in my grandmother's village near Sohag. As a child, I loved almost everything about those __[1] visits:__ the cool mud-brick house, the palm trees along the canal and the donkeys that carried clover home from the fields. What I loved most, however, was the morning my grandmother let my cousin Hoda and I help her bake.
The bread she made was called aish shamsi, or "sun bread", because the dough rises in the heat of the sun before it is baked. The night before, she mixed the dough in a wide clay bowl and leaves it to rest. In the morning, she shaped it into round loaves and set them on wooden trays in the courtyard. For an hour or more, the loaves sat in the sunshine, slowly rising and growing larger in size.
My job was to guard the trays from the chickens, which seemed to believe that the bread had been put out especially for them. Nevertheless, by the time the loaves were ready for the oven, I had chased the same red hen across the courtyard at least a dozen times.
The oven was a dome of mud and brick on the roof, heated with dried palm leaves and corn stalks. When my grandmother opened it's small iron door, a wave of heat rushed out and made my eyes water. She slid the loaves inside with a long wooden paddle, and within minutes they puffed up and turned golden brown. The smell that filled the roof was super awesome.
Years later, I can buy bread from any bakery in Cairo, but none of it tastes quite like my grandmothers. Perhaps that is because no bakery can sell the one ingredient hers always had: a whole summer morning spent in the sun beside her.

**Bread in the Sun**
Every summer, my family left Cairo to spend a month in my grandmother's village near Sohag. As a child, I loved almost everything about those visits: the cool mud-brick house, the palm trees along the canal and the donkeys that carried clover home from the fields. What I loved most, however, was the morning my grandmother let my cousin Hoda and I help her bake.
The bread she made was called aish shamsi, or "sun bread", because the dough rises in the heat of the sun before it is baked. The night before, she mixed the dough in a wide clay bowl and leaves it to rest. In the morning, she shaped it into round loaves and set them on wooden trays in the courtyard. For an hour or more, the loaves sat in the sunshine, slowly rising and growing larger in size.
My job was to guard the trays from the chickens, __[6] which seemed__ to believe that the bread had been put out especially for them. Nevertheless, by the time the loaves were ready for the oven, I had chased the same red hen across the courtyard at least a dozen times.
The oven was a dome of mud and brick on the roof, heated with dried palm leaves and corn stalks. When my grandmother opened it's small iron door, a wave of heat rushed out and made my eyes water. She slid the loaves inside with a long wooden paddle, and within minutes they puffed up and turned golden brown. The smell that filled the roof was super awesome.
Years later, I can buy bread from any bakery in Cairo, but none of it tastes quite like my grandmothers. Perhaps that is because no bakery can sell the one ingredient hers always had: a whole summer morning spent in the sun beside her.

**Passage 1 (Literary fiction).** This passage is adapted from an original short story. It is set in a farming village in the Nile Delta in the middle of the twentieth century.
**Keeping the Water**
[1] In the village of Kafr el-Nakhl the water came by turns, and that summer it was the turn of the Mansour family to receive it at night. The canal that fed the fields was shared by eleven families, and the old agreement, older than anyone could remember, gave each of them so many hours of water in the week. Some received it in the morning, when the air was soft and the egrets stood along the banks like folded letters. The Mansours, by the ill luck of the drawing, received theirs from midnight until dawn.
[2] Karim was twelve, and he had never before been allowed to keep the water. That was his father's work, and before his father it had been his grandfather's, and Karim had watched it only from the doorway of the house: a lantern swinging away into the dark and returning, hours later, with a man too tired to speak. But in June his father had cut his hand on a sickle, and the wound, though it was healing, would not bear the weight of a hoe. "You will go," his father said at supper, and went on eating, as if he had asked for the salt.
[3] The fields at night were not the fields Karim knew. By day they were his own country; he could have walked from the house to the canal with his eyes shut, counting the palms. Now the palms had vanished into the sky, and the path, which had always been straight, seemed to bend in places where no bend had ever been. Frogs called from every ditch. Somewhere a dog barked once and was silent, and the silence afterwards was worse than the bark.
[4] He found the little sluice gate where his father had told him it would be, and he lifted the board as he had seen it lifted a hundred times. For a moment nothing happened. Then the water came, black and quick, whispering into the first channel, and Karim felt something loosen in his chest. He walked beside it with his lantern, breaking the small earth walls with his hoe to let the water into each square of the field and building them up again when the square was full. It was slow work, and he did it slowly, for his father had said that a field watered in haste is a field watered twice.
[5] It was nearly three o'clock when he heard the sound of a spade further up the bank. He raised the lantern and saw old Hajj Saber, whose fields lay beside their own, cutting a narrow opening in the canal wall. The water, which should have been running to the Mansours until dawn, had begun to slip sideways into the Hajj's land.
[6] Karim stood very still. Hajj Saber was the oldest man on their side of the village; at weddings he sat in the first chair, and boys of twelve did not speak to him unless he spoke first. Karim thought of turning back and pretending he had seen nothing. Then he thought of his father's hand, wrapped in its white cloth, and of the cotton plants, which had already waited a week for this water.
[7] "Good evening, Hajj," he said. His voice came out higher than he wished, and he began again. "Good evening. It is our turn until the morning prayer."
[8] The old man straightened slowly and looked at him for a long time across the lantern light. Karim could not read his face. Then, to the boy's astonishment, the Hajj laughed: a short, dry sound, like a stick breaking.
[9] "So it is," he said. "Your grandfather would have said the same, and in the same voice." He bent, closed the opening with three strokes of the spade and pressed the earth down with his foot. "I only wanted to see," he added, more to himself than to Karim, "who was keeping the water tonight."
[10] He went away along the bank without another word. Karim watched the lantern in the old man's window until it went out. Then he turned back to the field, where the water was still running, and walked beside it until the sky above the palms grew pale and the first birds began, one after another, to speak.
questions.q: Which choice best summarises the passage?
c: A boy who takes over his father's night-time duty of watering the family's fields politely stands up to an elder who is diverting the water.
Two families quarrel over the village's water agreement until the elders change it.
A boy gets lost in the dark fields and is guided home by an old neighbour.
A boy finishes his own work early and then helps an old neighbour water his fields.
questions.e: The story follows Karim's first night keeping the water and his decision to speak to Hajj Saber, who closes the opening. The other choices invent events (getting lost, a quarrel, helping the neighbour) that do not happen.
ce: This covers the whole story: the new duty, the night fields, the meeting with Hajj Saber and Karim's polite challenge.
There is no quarrel between families and the agreement is never changed.
Karim finds the sluice gate and stays in the field until dawn; he is never lost or guided home.
Karim does not help Hajj Saber; he stops him taking the Mansours' water.

**Passage 2 (History and social studies).** This passage is adapted from an original article about a voting custom in ancient Athens.
**Voting Someone Out**
[1] In the early fifth century BC, the citizens of Athens took part in one of the strangest elections in history. Instead of choosing a leader, they chose a man to send away. Each voter scratched a name on a broken piece of pottery, and if enough votes were cast, the man whose name appeared most often had to leave the city for ten years. The pieces of pottery were called ostraka, and the practice became known as ostracism, a word that English still uses for shutting someone out of a group.
[2] The procedure was carefully controlled. Once a year, the Assembly, the gathering of all citizens, voted on a simple question: should an ostracism be held this year? Nobody was named at this stage. If the majority said yes, the vote itself took place some weeks later in the Agora, the city's main public square, where an area was fenced off and voters entered tribe by tribe. Ancient writers agree that six thousand votes were needed, but they disagree about what that meant: some say six thousand votes had to be cast in total, while others say that six thousand had to be cast against a single man.
[3] Ostracism was not a punishment for a crime, and in some ways it was surprisingly mild. The man who was sent away kept his property and his citizenship, and when his ten years were over he could return to Athens with his honour untouched. Some ostracised men were even recalled early when the city needed their skills in a war. The purpose, it seems, was less to punish than to prevent. Athens had only recently freed itself from rule by tyrants, and many citizens feared that a single ambitious man might gather enough power to seize the city again. Ostracism gave the people a peaceful way to remove such a man before he became dangerous.
[4] In practice, however, the system could be used for other ends. Rival politicians sometimes campaigned to have each other removed, and a vote could become a contest between two leaders and their supporters. A well-known story told by the later writer Plutarch shows how personal the process could be. A voter who could not write handed his piece of pottery to a stranger and asked him to write the name Aristides on it. The stranger, who was Aristides himself, asked what harm Aristides had done. The man replied that he did not even know Aristides; he was simply tired of hearing everyone call him "the Just". Aristides, the story goes, wrote his own name and handed the piece back.
[5] Archaeologists have found thousands of ostraka in Athens, and they offer a rare glimpse of ordinary citizens taking part in politics. Most are scratched in many different hands, with spelling that varies from voter to voter. One group, however, has puzzled and fascinated scholars. Found together, nearly two hundred pieces bear the name of the statesman Themistocles, yet they appear to have been written by only a small number of people. They may have been prepared in advance and handed out to voters, perhaps to help citizens who could not write, or perhaps by opponents hoping to influence the result. Whatever their purpose, they suggest that organised campaigns are not a modern invention.
[6] Ostracism did not last. The last known ostracism took place around 416 BC, and its result was unexpected. According to ancient accounts, two rival leaders, each in danger of being sent away, combined their supporters' votes against a third, less important politician named Hyperbolus, who was ostracised instead. After that, the Athenians seem to have lost faith in the practice, and although the law was never formally removed, it was not used again.
[7] Today, ostracism is often remembered as an example of how a democracy can treat talented individuals unfairly. Yet it can also be read as an early attempt to solve a problem that every free society faces: how to keep power from collecting in the hands of one person without turning to violence. The Athenians' answer was imperfect, but the question they asked has never gone away.

telling the life story of the statesman Aristides.

**Passage 3 (Science).** This passage is adapted from an original article about growing crops beneath solar panels. The study described is fictional, and its data are for practice only.
**Two Harvests from One Field**
[1] Solar farms need space, and so do ordinary farms. In many countries, the two compete for the same flat, sunny land, and every field covered with panels is a field that no longer grows food. A growing number of researchers, however, have begun to ask whether the competition is necessary at all. What if crops could grow underneath the panels, so that a single field produced both electricity and food? The idea, known as agrivoltaics, sounds almost too convenient to be true. In hot, dry regions, it may turn out to be one of the most sensible ways of using land.
[2] At first glance, the plan seems to have an obvious flaw. Plants need sunlight to grow, and solar panels are designed to capture as much of that sunlight as they can. Yet many crops receive more sunlight in a desert summer than they can actually use. Beyond a certain point, extra light does them little good, while the heat that comes with it dries out the soil and stresses the leaves. For such plants, a little shade may be less a sacrifice than a relief.
[3] To test this idea, a team led by agricultural engineer Nadia Fawzy grew tomatoes on an experimental farm on the edge of the desert. The team divided the farm into four plots of equal size. One plot was left as an open field. Over the other three, the researchers mounted solar panels on frames three metres high, tall enough for workers and small machines to pass underneath. The panels were spaced at different distances, so that each plot received a different amount of shade. All four plots were watered by the same drip system, which recorded exactly how much water each one used over the growing season. The results are shown in the table.
Table: Shade, tomato harvest and water use in four plots
Plot | Shade from panels (% of daylight blocked) | Tomato harvest (kilograms) | Water used per kilogram of tomatoes (litres)
Open field | 0 | 410 | 62
Widely spaced panels | 20 | 432 | 51
Medium-spaced panels | 35 | 418 | 45
Closely spaced panels | 55 | 305 | 41
[4] Moderate shade did not harm the harvest; in fact, the plot with widely spaced panels produced slightly more tomatoes than the open field. Only under the closely spaced panels, where more than half the daylight was blocked, did the harvest fall sharply. Water use told a simpler story. The more shade a plot received, the less water was needed to grow each kilogram of tomatoes, because the shaded soil lost less moisture to evaporation.
[5] The benefits ran in both directions. Solar panels work less efficiently when they become very hot, and on summer afternoons the panels in an ordinary solar farm nearby often grew too hot to touch. Over the tomato plots, the moisture released by the leaves cooled the air beneath the panels. Fawzy's team found that the panels above the crops produced slightly more electricity per panel than identical panels mounted over bare ground. "The plants cool the panels, and the panels shade the plants," Fawzy says. "Each one makes the other work a little better."
[6] The researchers are careful not to claim too much. Their study lasted only one season and involved only one crop; leafy vegetables and grains may respond differently to shade, and a wetter or cooler climate could change the results entirely. Building tall frames also costs more than placing panels directly on the ground. Fawzy believes, however, that the findings point to a future in which the question is no longer whether land should be used for food or for energy. "In the right places," she says, "we may be able to have both."

**Passage 4 (Paired texts).** Text 1 and Text 2 are original opinion pieces about whether a country should try to grow all of its own food.
**Text 1**
[1] A country that cannot feed itself is never fully in control of its own future. When food must cross oceans to reach the table, every storm, war or quarrel between distant governments becomes a threat to the family meal. When shipping routes are blocked or a major exporter suddenly stops selling grain abroad, prices in importing countries can rise within weeks, and the poorest families feel the shock first.
[2] Growing more of our own food is the surest protection against such shocks. It also keeps money and skills at home. Every tonne of wheat grown by local farmers supports village families, rural shops and the mills and bakeries that depend on them. When a country relies on imports, those jobs move abroad, and young people leave the countryside for crowded cities in search of work.
[3] Critics say that some crops are simply too expensive to grow at home. That may be true in a narrow sense, but cost is not the only measure of value. A family buys insurance not because it expects disaster every year but because it cannot afford to be unprepared when disaster comes. Investment in local farming, from better seeds to modern irrigation, is that kind of insurance. **Passage 5 (Humanities).** This passage is adapted from an original essay about the history of paper.
**The Quiet Invention**
[1] Of all the inventions that changed the way people think, paper may be the least noticed. We write shopping lists on it, wrap food in it and throw it away by the armful, rarely pausing to consider that for most of human history it did not exist. Yet without paper, the spread of books, schools, newspapers and even paper money would have been slow and costly, if it had happened at all. The story of this quiet invention begins in China, nearly two thousand years ago.
[2] Before paper, Chinese writers had two main choices, and neither was convenient. They could write on strips of bamboo, tied together with cord into bundles that could be rolled up. Bamboo was cheap, but it was heavy: a single long work might fill a cart. Alternatively, they could write on silk, which was light and smooth but far too expensive for everyday use. What was needed was a material with the lightness of silk and the cheapness of bamboo.

questions.q: The author's remark that printing books on parchment "would have required the skins of entire herds" (paragraph [5]) suggests that
c: farmers in Europe raised animals mainly for parchment.
parchment was cheaper than paper in the fifteenth century.
large-scale printing would have been impractical without cheap paper.
printers preferred parchment to paper.
questions.e: The image of whole herds shows how unrealistic it would have been to print thousands of books on animal skin, so cheap paper was essential. Nothing suggests printers preferred parchment.
ce: The remark is about what printing would have needed, not about farming.
The remark shows parchment would have been very costly in large quantities.
So many animals would be needed that mass printing on parchment was unrealistic.
The passage says printing depended on paper.

questions.p:
**Passage 5 (Humanities).** This passage is adapted from an original essay about the history of paper.
**The Quiet Invention**
[1] Of all the inventions that changed the way people think, paper may be the least noticed. We write shopping lists on it, wrap food in it and throw it away by the armful, rarely pausing to consider that for most of human history it did not exist. Yet without paper, the spread of books, schools, newspapers and even paper money would have been slow and costly, if it had happened at all. The story of this quiet invention begins in China, nearly two thousand years ago.
[2] Before paper, Chinese writers had two main choices, and neither was convenient. They could write on strips of bamboo, tied together with cord into bundles that could be rolled up. Bamboo was cheap, but it was heavy: a single long work might fill a cart. Alternatively, they could write on silk, which was light and smooth but far too expensive for everyday use. What was needed was a material with the lightness of silk and the cheapness of bamboo.
[3] Chinese tradition gives credit for that material to Cai Lun, an official at the court of the Han emperor, who in the year 105 CE is said to have presented the emperor with a new kind of writing surface. According to the official history of the dynasty, he made it from tree bark, hemp, old rags and worn-out fishing nets, beaten into a pulp, spread thin and dried. Archaeologists have since found fragments of paper that appear to be older than Cai Lun's time, so he was probably not the first person to make it. His achievement, it seems, was to improve the process and to win official support for it, turning a little-known craft into a practical material.
[4] For several centuries, papermaking remained largely a Chinese skill. It spread first to China's neighbours, including Korea and Japan, and then, more slowly, westward. By the end of the eighth century, paper was being made in Baghdad, the capital of the Abbasid caliphate, and from there the craft moved across the Islamic world, reaching Egypt, North Africa and, eventually, Muslim Spain. In each new place, paper did not simply replace older materials; it changed what people could afford to write. Government offices kept more records, scholars copied more books, and libraries grew to sizes that would have been unthinkable when every page had to be cut from an animal skin or made from a reed plant.
[5] It was only after this long journey that paper reached most of Christian Europe, where it was at first regarded with some suspicion. Parchment, made from animal skin, was thought to be more durable, and some rulers insisted that important documents be written on it. Paper's great advantage, however, was its cost. When printing with movable type spread across Europe in the fifteenth century, it depended on a cheap supply of paper; printing thousands of books on parchment would have required the skins of entire herds.
[6] Today, as more of our reading moves to screens, it is tempting to think that paper's long reign is ending. Perhaps it is. But the qualities that made Cai Lun's material so valuable (its lightness, its cheapness and its readiness to carry any word that anyone cared to write) are exactly the qualities we now expect from our devices. In that sense, the digital page is less a replacement for paper than its latest descendant.
questions.q: The author describes the digital page as paper's "latest descendant" (paragraph [6]) mainly to suggest that
c: Cai Lun also invented early forms of digital devices.
modern devices continue the purposes that made paper valuable.
screens will never replace paper in any form.
paper and screens have nothing in common.
questions.e: The author lists paper's key qualities and says we expect the same from devices, so screens carry on paper's role. The word "descendant" does not mean the two have nothing in common or that Cai Lun invented devices.
ce: This is a literal misreading of a figure of speech.
Lightness, cheapness and the ability to carry any word are the same qualities we expect of screens.
The author allows that paper's reign may be ending ("Perhaps it is").
The author says they share the same valued qualities.
